tahajjud.summary: The night prayer offered in the last third of the night, before Fajr.
tahajjud.why: Allah descends to the lowest heaven in the last third of the night and asks who will call upon Him. The Prophet ﷺ regularly prayed at night even when optional for him.
tahajjud.benefits: Draws one closer to Allah, softens the heart, and was the habit of the righteous before him. A time when du'a is especially answered.

fajr.summary: The dawn prayer — the first of the five daily obligatory prayers.
fajr.why: Allah commanded establishing prayer at the edges of the day; Fajr marks the start of the Muslim day and was never abandoned by the Prophet ﷺ in congregation or alone.
fajr.benefits: Whoever prays Fajr is under Allah's protection. It is witnessed by the angels of the night and day and brings light for the rest of the day.

sunrise.summary: The moment the sun rises above the horizon — a time marker, not a prayer itself.
sunrise.why: Prayer is forbidden while the sun is rising (and at zenith and setting) so the ummah does not resemble sun-worshippers. Knowing sunrise helps time Ishraq and avoid invalid prayer times.
sunrise.benefits: Observing Allah's signs in the sky increases awe (taqwa) and helps structure the morning sunnah prayers correctly.

ishraq.summary: A two-rak'ah sunnah prayer after the sun has fully risen (about 15–20 minutes after sunrise).
ishraq.why: The Prophet ﷺ said whoever prays Fajr in congregation then sits remembering Allah until sunrise, then prays two rak'ahs, receives the reward of a complete Hajj and 'Umrah.
ishraq.benefits: Immense reward with minimal effort when combined with Fajr in congregation. A peaceful start to the day in dhikr and optional prayer.

duha.summary: The forenoon prayer — typically two to eight rak'ahs between sunrise and Dhuhr.
duha.why: Charity is due on every joint of the body each day; even a few rak'ahs of Duha fulfills that charity for the limbs through worship.
duha.benefits: Forgives sins, brings sustenance (rizq), and revives a neglected sunnah. Flexible timing makes it accessible when the day allows.

dhuhr.summary: The midday prayer — the second obligatory prayer, when the sun passes its zenith.
dhuhr.why: The five daily prayers were made obligatory on the Night Journey; Dhuhr breaks the day's busyness with remembrance of Allah.
dhuhr.benefits: The Prophet ﷺ said the first deed judged on the Day of Resurrection is prayer. Guarding Dhuhr protects the rest of one's deeds.

asr.summary: The afternoon prayer — the middle prayer emphasized in the Qur'an.
asr.why: Allah specifically warns about guarding the middle prayer (Salat al-Wusta). It falls when many are busy or tired, so preserving it is a sign of sincerity.
asr.benefits: Whoever misses Asr, it is as if he lost his family and wealth — highlighting its weight. Keeping it strengthens discipline through the day.

maghrib.summary: The sunset prayer — prayed immediately after the sun has set.
maghrib.why: The time opens right at sunset; delaying without reason risks missing the preferred window. The Prophet ﷺ warned against neglecting prayer until the sun has set.
maghrib.benefits: Marks gratitude at the day's end and was among the first prayers the Prophet ﷺ emphasized to his companions.

isha.summary: The night prayer — the last of the five obligatory prayers, after twilight fades.
isha.why: Completes the cycle of daily worship. The Prophet ﷺ said if someone prayed Isha in congregation, it is as if he prayed half the night.
isha.benefits: Brings tranquility before sleep, completes the day's obligations, and pairs naturally with Witr for those who follow that sunnah.

witr.summary: An odd-numbered prayer (usually one or three rak'ahs) after Isha before Fajr.
witr.why: The Prophet ﷺ said Allah is Witr (One) and loves Witr, so maintain the Witr prayer. He never abandoned it, even when traveling.
witr.benefits: A distinctive mark of the believer's night routine. Closing the day with odd-numbered prayer aligns with Allah's names and the Prophet's consistent practice.

tahiyyatul_masjid.summary: Two rak'ahs greeting the mosque when entering, before sitting.
tahiyyatul_masjid.why: When one of you enters the mosque, let him pray two rak'ahs before sitting — a direct instruction of the Prophet ﷺ.
tahiyyatul_masjid.benefits: Honors the house of Allah, prepares the heart for congregation or private worship, and replaces idle sitting with immediate good.

hajat_istikhara.summary: Optional prayers for personal needs (Salat al-Hajah) and seeking Allah's guidance (Salat al-Istikhara).
hajat_istikhara.why: Istikhara is to ask Allah to choose good for you when facing a decision. Hajah is to present one's need to Allah through prayer before or alongside du'a.
hajat_istikhara.benefits: Builds reliance on Allah (tawakkul) instead of anxiety alone. Istikhara brings clarity; Hajah pairs worship with sincere request — and Allah answers those who call upon Him.

witrNote.title: Is Witr qaza required?
witrNote.intro: According to the majority of scholars, making up a missed Witr is allowed, but whether it is required depends on your madhhab (school of thought).
witrNote.hanafiBody: Witr is wajib (obligatory). If you miss it, you must make it up (qada'). Pray it as soon as you remember — even if days or weeks have passed. This is the view followed by most Muslims in South Asia, Central Asia, and Turkey.
witrNote.othersBody: Witr is a strongly emphasized sunnah (sunnah mu'akkadah), not obligatory. Making it up is recommended (mustahabb) but not required. The Prophet ﷺ would make up night prayers missed due to sleep or illness.
witrNote.evidenceBody: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever sleeps and misses Witr or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers." (Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah — scholars differ on its grading.) In Sahih Muslim, when he missed night prayer due to illness or sleep, he made it up during the day with an even number of rak'ahs.
witrNote.footer: This app counts missed Witr toward qaza for all users. Treat it as required if you follow the Hanafi view; otherwise track it as a recommended make-up. Consult a scholar for your situation.

note.whiteDaysBody: The 13th, 14th, and 15th of each Islamic month fall around the full moon. Fasting these three bright days is a beloved sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ.
note.newMonthBody: The thin crescent (hilāl) marks the start of {{month}}. Each Islamic month begins when the new moon is first sighted after sunset.
note.fullBody: The moon is fully lit near the middle of {{month}} — the nights of the White Days, when fasting is especially recommended.
note.generalBody: The Islamic (Hijri) calendar follows the moon: every month is 29 or 30 days, beginning with the sighting of the new crescent.
